latin: Mactī<sup>1</sup> virtūte ēstote<sup>2</sup>, vōs quī usque ad hanc ultimam lēctiōnem pervēnistis!
Sī in hīs lēctiōnibus prōsequendīs prōpositum discendī modum servāvimus,
multa trītissimaque<sup>3</sup> verba nōbīs quasi amīcī et familiārēs factī sunt;
variārum sententiārum exempla in auribus nostrīs impressa sunt;
ipsīus dēnique grammaticae jam nōn omnīnō ignārī sumus.
Attamen, sī lingua latīnā nōbīs amīca facta est, ad meliōra etiam nunc prōgredī possumus.
Nam prīmum usque ad librī fīnem «undam alteram» pervolvēmus<sup>4</sup>.
Praetereā cotīdiē librum quālibet pāginā aperiēmus, lēctiōnēs quāsdam relegēmus, annotātiōnēs iterum cōnsulēmus<sup>5</sup>, discōs iterum audiēmus,
dōnec<sup>6</sup> omnia, quae hoc in librō invenīrī possunt, sine ūllā animī contentiōne<sup>7</sup> capiēmus.
Posteā ultrā pergendum erit, sine hāc conversiōnum annotātiōnumque fultūrā<sup>8</sup>, quae nōbīs hūc usque numquam dēfuit.
Per nōs ipsōs jam inveniāmus oportēbit, librōs, documenta, praecepta, atque etiam amīcōs, quī nōbīs ad haec comparanda, vel colloquiīs vel epistulīs, auxilium dent<sup>9</sup>.
Ēos librōs, exemplī grātiā, nōbīs comparāre poterimus quōrum excerpta in hōc opere posita magis placuērunt.
Sī librōs lēgerīmus, eōs legendō tālēs stimulōs<sup>10</sup> ad novōs librōs vel commentāriōs legendōs inveniēmus, ut legenda numquam nōs dēficere possint.
Grammatica vērō, quamquam saepe ejus rēgulīs potior est<sup>11</sup> ūsus, nōn tamen omnīnō ac temere neglegenda est.

Prīmum igitur appendicem<sup>12</sup> grammaticālem, quae in ultimīs librī pāginīs continētur, iterum iterumque revolvēmus<sup>13</sup>, posteā autem ūtile erit accūrātiora complētioraque opera cōnsulere<sup>14</sup>.
Quā in rē, hujus cōnsiliī semper meminisse dēbēmus:

Artem āctīvam, quae in latīne loquendō, latīne legendō, latīne scrībendō, latīne cōgitandō cōnsistit, et doctrīnam, qua morphologiam et syntaxim<sup>15</sup> intellegere possumus, semper inter sē conjungere et cōpulāre dēbēmus.
Hīs praeceptīs fretī, aeronautārum prōverbium nōbīs audācter arripiāmus: per ardua ad astra...
Nunc vestrīs vīribus cōnfīsī, ipsī fēlīciter ēvolētis!
Valēte, Optimī Lēctōrēs, et linguam nostram amāte!
latinAccented: Mactī<sup>1</sup> virtū́te ḗstote<sup>2</sup>, vōs quī usque ad hanc últimam lēctiṓnem pervēnístis!
Sī in hīs lēctiṓnibus prōsequéndīs prōpósitum discéndī modum servā́vimus,
multa trītissimáque<sup>3</sup> verba nōbīs quasi amī́cī et familiā́rēs factī sunt;
variā́rum sententiā́rum exémpla in áuribus nostrīs impréssa sunt;
ipsī́us dḗnique grammáticae jam nōn omnī́nō ignā́rī sumus.
Áttamen, sī lingua latī́nā nōbīs amī́ca facta est, ad meliṓra étiam nunc prṓgredī póssumus.
Nam prīmum usque ad librī fīnem «undam álteram» pervolvḗmus<sup>4</sup>.
Praetéreā cotī́diē librum quā́libet pā́ginā aperiḗmus, lēctiṓnēs quāsdam relegḗmus, annotātiṓnēs íterum cōnsulḗmus<sup>5</sup>, discōs íterum audiḗmus,
dōnec<sup>6</sup> ómnia, quae hoc in librō invenī́rī possunt, sine ūllā ánimī contentiṓne<sup>7</sup> capiḗmus.
Pósteā ultrā pergéndum erit, sine hāc conversiṓnum annotātiōnúmque fultū́rā<sup>8</sup>, quae nōbīs hūc usque numquam dḗfuit.
Per nōs ipsōs jam inveniā́mus oportḗbit, librōs, documénta, praecépta, atque étiam amī́cōs, quī nōbīs ad haec comparánda, vel collóquiīs vel epístulīs, auxílium dent<sup>9</sup>.
Ēos librōs, exémplī grā́tiā, nōbīs comparā́re potérimus quōrum excérpta in hōc ópere pósita magis placuḗrunt.
Sī librōs lēgerī́mus, eōs legéndō tālēs stímulōs<sup>10</sup> ad novōs librōs vel commentā́riōs legéndōs inveniḗmus, ut legénda numquam nōs dēfícere possint.
Grammática vērō, quamquam saepe ejus rḗgulīs pótior est<sup>11</sup> ūsus, nōn tamen omnī́nō ac témere neglegénda est.

Prīmum ígitur appéndicem<sup>12</sup> grammaticā́lem, quae in últimīs librī pā́ginīs continḗtur, íterum iterúmque revolvḗmus<sup>13</sup>, pósteā autem ū́tile erit accūrātíora complētioráque ópera cōnsúlere<sup>14</sup>.
Quā in rē, hujus cōnsíliī semper meminísse dēbḗmus:

Artem āctī́vam, quae in latī́ne loquéndō, latī́ne legéndō, latī́ne scrībéndō, latī́ne cōgitándō cōnsístit, et doctrī́nam, qua morphológiam et syntáxim<sup>15</sup> intellégere póssumus, semper inter sē conjúngere et cōpulā́re dēbḗmus.
Hīs praecéptīs fretī, aeronautā́rum prōvérbium nōbīs audā́cter arripiā́mus: per árdua ad astra...
Nunc vestrīs vī́ribus cōnfī́sī, ipsī fēlī́citer ēvolḗtis!
Valḗte, Óptimī Lēctṓrēs, et linguam nostram amā́te!
english: [Good luck] (be glorified by your virtue), you who have come to the end of this last lesson!
If [in] (pursuing) these lessons we have followed the [method] proposed (means of learning),
many [very common] words have become [for us] like friends and familiars;
examples of different sentences are imprinted in [our auditory memory] (our ears);
and finally we are not completely ignorant of grammar itself.
But however, if the Latin language has become [our friend] (friend to us), we can still now [progress] towards better things.
For first we will [pursue] the «second wave» to the end of the book ([we will] roll).

In addition every day we will open the book at [any page at all] (whatever page) [taken at random], we will reread certain lessons, we will consult the notes again and we will listen to the records again,
until the moment when [we understand without effort] all the things which can be found in this book ([without any tension of the mind we will grasp]).
Then it will be necessary to go further, without this support of the translations and of the notes, which up to now has never been lacking to us.

From now on it will be necessary that we find for ourselves the books, the documents, the advice, and also the friends who [will help] us to procure these things, whether by conversation(s) or by letters (help that they give).
For example we will be able to procure [the] books whose extracts [encountered] (placed) in this work have pleased us more.
If we [read] (will have read) books, in reading them we will find such stimulants to read new books or reviews that never the [reading] (things to read) will be able to be lacking to us.
As for grammar, although often usage prevails over its rules, it must nevertheless not be totally and lightly neglected.

So at the start [it is] the grammatical appendix, which [is] (is contained) in the last pages of the book, [that] we will reread [several times] (again and again), but then it will be useful to consult more precise and more complete works.
In this matter we must always remember this advice:

The [practice] (active art), which consists in speaking in Latin, reading in Latin, writing in Latin, thinking in Latin, and the theory, by which we can understand morphology and syntax, we must always link and associate them (between themselves).
Strengthened by these counsels, [let us not be afraid to make our own] the proverb of the aviators (for us audaciously let us seize): [it is] by rough [paths] [that one climbs] towards the stars...
And now, trusting in [your] (your) strength(s), [make a good flight] on your own wings (that you may yourselves fly away happily)!
Goodbye, valiant readers, and love our language!

footnotes: Mactus, -a, -um (adjective which is only used in the nominative and the masculine and feminine vocative) means honoured. Example of the masculine singular vocative: macte animo, generose puer! courage, child of (good) race (genus, -eris, n.)!

Estote, future imperative of esse. We have tried not to bore you too much with the analysis of the tenses and moods. Now we advise you to refer frequently to the GRAMMATICAL APPENDIX, until you possess perfectly all the active, passive and deponent forms.

From which verb comes tritus? — Answer: E. 59 (notes).

N.B. — At the end of the phrase, amica et familiaria facta sunt, one should have [grammatically] familiares (neuter), had been grammatically correct, but the masculine agreement of the verb and of the predicate shows us that these friends now have a more marked personality than that which «things» would have.
Pervolvere, to roll (or to make roll) entirely; but also to read assiduously, for you remember that the book was formerly a roll: volumen. Volvo, -is, -ere, i, utum, to roll or to make roll.
Consulo, -is, -ere, sului, sultum, to hold counsel, to examine, to consult.
Donec, conj., which we have already seen (L. 45, N. 5), but which you will find again in the grammatical appendix, § 49.

Contentio, -onis, f., tension, effort. This effort, we have made it carried above all on vocabulary. In this book, you have found about 3,000 different words. When by dint of REPETITIONS you know them all, you will be able to READ any current text WITHOUT A DICTIONARY and understand, at least approximately, what it is about. That is already an ENORMOUS FORCE which too many Latinists neglect wrongly. But to maintain and increase this possibility, you must not be afraid of READING A LOT, even if you do not always understand perfectly what you read. It is only when you have accumulated the essentials of this capital that the use of the DICTIONARY and of GRAMMAR will become perfectly productive. We do not hide from you that you will need these TWO AIDS if you want to appreciate fully the good authors, or quite simply if you want to speak and write correctly.

To find these correspondents, one solution consists in sending your name and your address to a Latin review having a section for this purpose. With a bit of luck someone will write to you. But do not forget that, for correspondence, it is with Latin as with other living languages: great perseverance is necessary, experience showing that few correspondents are capable of maintaining a durable commercium epistulare. So do not worry if your first efforts are not crowned with success, for it is improbable that larks will fall to you all roasted: nulli per ventos assa columba volat, for no one (dat. of nullus) does the roast pigeon fly with the winds.

Stimulus, -i, m., lit. the goad, for pricking (stimulare) oxen. The goad of insects is said aculeus, -i, m. (acus, the needle) or cuspis, -idis, f. We are not oxen, but we sometimes need a STIMULANT! When a book has interested us, have we not wanted to read the continuation if there is one, or another book by the same author, or yet other books on the same subject, whether they are or not explicitly cited by the author. Let us remind you that in most books, one finds, apart from the text proper, quantities of information to this effect (preface, notes, appendices, end pages, etc.).
Potior, -ius, comparative of potis, -e (cf. L. 99, N. 6).
Appendix, -icis, f., object suspended from... (appendo = ad pendo, to suspend); accessory, dependency. Note that the gender is not the same as in French.
Revolvere, to roll backwards, to run through again. We gave revolt, revolution, and even revolver! (cf. N. 4 supra).

May our imperfect work give you this desire for perfection which was one of the traits of Caesar's character! LUCAN said of him:
... nil actum credens cum quid superesset agendum...
... thinking that nothing was done when there remained something to do... (Pharsalia, II, 657).
But let us not transform this desire for perfection into an isolated pride, and let us listen, always through Lucan, to this precept of Cato of Utica:
Nec sibi sed toti genitum se credere mundo
and not to believe himself born for himself [alone] but for the entire world (Pharsalia, II, 383).

Syntaxis, -is, f.: words in -is of Greek origin often have the accusative singular in im and the ablative singular in i. For the case where you would not know it, you will learn without difficulty the sense of the words morphology and syntax by reading the GRAMMATICAL APPENDIX.
comments: This lesson and these notes are more particularly intended to conclude the 2nd wave. If you read them for the first time, pay above all your attention to phrases 1 to 9.
